label: prop:complementary-slackness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:complementary-slackness}
    Let $q \in \mathcal{Q}$ such that ${v_\infty}(q) = \frac{1}{K_G}$.
    Let $\mu$ be a distribution on $f,g : \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \{-1,1\}$ such that $c_1(\mu) \geq \frac{1}{K_G} - \varepsilon$ and $\sum_{\textnormal{odd }m \geq 3} |c_m(\mu)| \leq \varepsilon$.
    Then $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{(f,g) \sim \mu}{\langle{f, Qg}\rangle} \geq \frac{1}{K_G} - 2\varepsilon.$

label: lem:hfg-analytic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hfg-analytic}
    Let $f,g : \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \{\pm1\}$ be measurable. Then $\sum_m |c_m(f,g)| \leq 1$. Thus, $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \ell_1$.
    The series for $H_{f,g}$ and $H_\mu$ converge absolutely
    and uniformly for $t \in \mathbb{C}, |t|\le1$ and are holomorphic for $|t|<1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall $c_i(f,g) = {\langle{\Pi_i f, \Pi_i g}\rangle}$.
    Using Cauchy--Schwarz twice,
    \[
        \sum_k |{\langle{\Pi_k f, \Pi_k g}\rangle}| \leq \sum_{k} \norm{\Pi_k f}_2 \norm{\Pi_k g}_2 \leq \left(\sum_k \norm{\Pi_k f}_2^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_k \norm{\Pi_k g}_2^2\right)^{1/2} = \norm{f}_2 \norm{g}_2 = 1\,.
    \]
    Then for a general $\mu$ we have $\sum_m|c_m(\mu)|
        \le\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{(f,g)\sim\mu}\sum_m|c_m(f,g)|\le1$.
    Absolute summability gives the stated convergence and holomorphy.

label: lem:odd-rounding
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:odd-rounding}
Let $q \in \mathcal{Q}$ and $Q = \sum_{\textnormal{odd }m \geq 1}q_m \Pi_m$. Then
\[
    \operatorname{OPT}(Q) = \sup_{f,g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \{\pm 1\}} \langle f, Qg\rangle = \sup_{\textnormal{odd }f,g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \{\pm1\}} \langle f, Qg\rangle\,.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given $f,g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \{\pm 1\}$ their odd parts $f_{\text{odd}}(X) = \frac{f(X) - f(-X)}{2}$ and $g_\text{odd}(X) = \frac{g(X) - g(-X)}{2}$
    satisfy $\langle f, Q g\rangle  = \langle f_{\text{odd}}, Qg_{\text{odd}}\rangle$.
    Furthermore, $f_{\text{odd}}(X), g_{\text{odd}}(X) \in \{-1,0,1\}$.

    Fix any odd Boolean function $a$, for example $a(X)=\operatorname{sign}(X_1)$. Define
    \[
     f_\pm=f_{\mathrm{odd}}\pm a\,\mathbf1_{\{f_{\mathrm{odd}}=0\}},
     \qquad
     g_\pm=g_{\mathrm{odd}}\pm a\,\mathbf1_{\{g_{\mathrm{odd}}=0\}}.
    \]
    These functions are odd and Boolean, and their respective averages
    are $f_{\mathrm{odd}}$ and $g_{\mathrm{odd}}$. Hence, ${\langle{f_\pm, Qg_\pm}\rangle} \geq {\langle{f_{\text{odd}}, Qg_{\text{odd}}}\rangle}$ for
    at least one of the four choices.
    Taking suprema proves the claim.

label: eq:tensor
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and let $u_i, v_j \in \ell_2, \norm{u_i} = \norm{v_j} = 1$ be an optimal SDP solution.
    Taking tensor powers shows
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:tensor}
        \left|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}{\langle{u_i,v_j}\rangle}^m\right|
        =\left|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}
        {\langle{u_i^{\otimes m},v_j^{\otimes m}}\rangle}\right|
        \le\operatorname{SDP}(A)\qquad(m\ge1).
    \end{equation}
    Let $\tilde{x}_i, \tilde{y}_j \in \{\pm 1\}$ be the randomized signs output by Gaussian rounding in \cref{eq:krivine-scheme}.
    We have
    \[
        \operatorname{OPT}(A) \geq \sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} \tilde x_i \tilde y_j = \sum_{i,j}A_{ij}H_\mu({\langle{u_i,v_j}\rangle})
        \overset{\text{\cref{eq:tensor}}}{\ge}\left(c_1(\mu)
        -\sum_{\substack{m\ge3\\m\textnormal{ odd}}}|c_m(\mu)|\right)
        \operatorname{SDP}(A).
    \]
    Therefore $\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(A)}{\operatorname{SDP}(A)} \geq c_1(\mu) - \sum_{\text{odd }m \geq 3} |c_m(\mu)|$ for all $A \ne 0$ which implies the same bound on $K_G^{-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:odd-rounding}, $v_\infty(q) = \sup_{c \in \mathcal{C}} {\langle{c,q}\rangle}$. We prove
    \[
        \frac{1}{K_G} \leq \inf\{v_\infty(q) : q \in \mathcal{Q}\} = \sup\Big\{c_1 - \sum_{\text{odd }m \geq 3}|c_m| : c \in \mathcal{C}\Big\} \leq \frac{1}{K_G}\,.
    \]
    The right inequality is \cref{lem:ub-easy}.
    The middle equality is convex duality. Indeed, $c_1 - \sum_{\text{odd }m \geq 3}|c_m| = \inf_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} {\langle{c,q}\rangle}$ for all $c \in \ell_1$.
    This implies the weak duality $\sup_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \inf_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} {\langle{c,q}\rangle} \leq \inf_{\substack{q \in \mathcal{Q}}} \sup_{c \in \mathcal{C}} {\langle{c,q}\rangle}$.
    Strong duality holds by Sion's minimax theorem: $\mathcal{C}$ is convex, $\mathcal{Q}$ is convex and compact in the weak-$^*$ topology on $\ell_\infty = (\ell_1)^*$,
    and ${\langle{c,q}\rangle}$ is affine and continuous in each variable separately.
    
    For the left inequality, let $q \in \mathcal{Q}$ and let $Q = \sum_m q_m \Pi_m^{(n)}$.
    Then $\operatorname{OPT}(Q) =  v_n(q) \leq {v_\infty}(q)$.
    On the other hand, $\operatorname{SDP}(Q) \geq 1-o_{n}(1)$ by $q_1 = 1$ and a standard estimate of the SDP value of the vector solution $f(x) = g(x) = \frac{x}{\norm{x}}$.
    Thus $\operatorname{SDP}(Q)/\operatorname{OPT}(Q) \geq \frac{1 - o_{n}(1)}{{v_\infty}(q)}$ and $K_G \geq \frac{1}{{v_\infty}(q)}$ as desired.

    We have that $v_\infty(q) = \sup_{c \in \mathcal{C}}{\langle{c,q}\rangle}$ is weak-$^*$ lower semicontinuous since it is a supremum of weak-$^*$ continuous functions.
    Then it attains a minimum on the weak-$^*$ compact set $\mathcal{Q}$.

label: ex:pi-d
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:pi-d}
Consider the Hermite projection matrix $\Pi_{d}^{(n)}$ with ${d} > 1$.
As $n \to \infty$, the $\infty$-to-1 norm of $\Pi_d$ is asymptotically achieved only by functions $f,g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \{\pm 1\}$ using a diverging number of variables, such as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-d}
    f(X) = g(X) = \operatorname{sign}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}}}\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \operatorname{He}_{d}(X_i)\right)
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{He}_d$ are the Hermite polynomials.
It can be shown that $f,g$ in \cref{eq:pi-d} are asymptotic optimizers of $\operatorname{OPT}(Q)$.
Calculating their value shows $\operatorname{SDP}(\Pi_{d})/\operatorname{OPT}(\Pi_{d}) = \frac{\pi}{2} - o_n(1)$. By the little Grothendieck inequality,
$\frac{\pi}{2}$ is the maximum possible integrality gap for PSD matrices.
The standard construction for little Grothendieck uses ${d}=1$ but it turns out that arbitrary ${d}$ has the same gap.

label: thm:closure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:closure}
Let $d_i\in \mathbb{N}$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item (Closure of the asymptotic space) Let $p_{n,i}\in\overline{\mathcal{H}}_{{d}_i}$ such that $\sup_n\norm{p_{n,i}}_2<\infty$ for all $i$.
    Then there exists a subsequence and $p_i\in\overline{\mathcal{H}}_{{d}_i}$ such that, along the subsequence, $(p_{n,i})_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\xrightarrow{d}(p_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$
    with convergence of all mixed (finite) moments.
    Consequently, $\{\textnormal{Law}(p):p\in\overline{\mathcal{H}}_{d}\}$ is weakly closed.

    \item (Approximability by finitary functions) For all $p_i \in \overline{\mathcal{H}}_{d_i}$
there exists a sequence $p_{n,i} \in \mathcal{H}_{d_i}(X_1, \dots, X_{n})$ such that $(p_{n,i})_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \xrightarrow{d} (p_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ with convergence of all mixed (finite) moments.
\end{enumerate}

label: lem:asymptotic-c
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:asymptotic-c}
Let $\mathcal K \subseteq \ell_1$ be the set of $c(\mu)$ for distributions $\mu$
on pairs of odd $f,g \in \overline{L_2}, f(X),g(X) \in \{\pm 1\}$.
Then $\mathcal K=\overline{\mathcal C}$ where $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ is the closure of $\mathcal{C}$ in $\ell_1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the auxiliary set
\[
 \mathcal B=
 \{c(f,g):f,g\in\overline{L_2}\text{ odd},\ |f|,|g|\le1\}.
\]

First we claim $\mathcal B \subseteq \mathcal K$.
Let $f,g \in \overline{L_2}$ odd, $|f|,|g|\le 1$.
We use an odd version of threshold rounding.
Let $a$ be any odd Boolean function, such as $a(X)=\operatorname{sign} X_1$.
For $s\in[-1,1]$, define
\[
 R_s h(X)=a(X)\operatorname{sign}\bigl(a(X)h(X)-s\bigr),
\]
with $\operatorname{sign}(0)=1$. If $h$ is odd and bounded by $1$, then
$R_s h$ is odd and Boolean, and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_sR_s h=h$ for uniform
$s\in[-1,1]$. Thus, for independent uniform $s,t$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:odd-threshold-rounding}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{s,t}c(R_s f,R_t g)=c(f,g).
\end{equation}
Thus $\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{K}$. The same proof shows that if odd $|f|,|g| \leq 1$ depend on only finitely many grade-one variables, then $c(f,g) \in \mathcal C$.

We next prove compactness of $\mathcal B$.
Take a sequence of odd $(f_n,g_n), |f_n|,|g_n| \leq 1$. By \cref{thm:closure}(i),
after passing to a subsequence there are
$p_d,r_d\in\overline{\mathcal H}_d$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ou-1}
 (\Pi_d f_n,\Pi_d g_n)_{d \in \mathbb{N}}
 \xrightarrow{d}(p_d,r_d)_{d\in \mathbb{N}}
\end{equation}
with convergence of the mixed moments of every finite
subtuple. For each fixed $D$,
\[\sum_{d \le D} \|p_d\|_2^2 = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{d \le D} \|\Pi_d f_n\|_2^2 \overset{\text{Parseval}}{\leq} 1\,.\]
Taking sup over $D$ shows $\sum_d\|p_d\|_2^2\le1$.
So $f=\sum_dp_d$ is well-defined in $\overline{L_2}$ and $\Pi_d f = p_d$.
The same holds for $g$.
Both are odd since their even-degree components vanish.

Note that we may \emph{not} have $f_n \xrightarrow{d} f$ since Hermite mass
for $f_n$ could escape to higher and higher degree.
We still prove $|f|,|g| \leq 1$. Fix $0<r<1$ and define the graded Ornstein--Uhlenbeck operator $T_r = \sum_d r^d \Pi_d$.
\cref{eq:ou-1} together with
\[
 \sup_n\left\|T_rf_n-\sum_{d\le D}r^d\Pi_df_n\right\|_2
 \le r^{D+1},
\]
implies $T_rf_n\xrightarrow{d}T_rf$.
For the nonnegative continuous function
$\varphi(x)=(|x|-1)_+$, the Portmanteau inequality gives
\[
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\varphi(T_rf)
 \le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\varphi(T_rf_n)=0,
\]
since $|T_rf_n|\le1$. Finally, $T_rf\to f$ in $L_2$
as $r\uparrow1$, and $\varphi$ is $1$-Lipschitz, so
$\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\varphi(f)=0$. Hence $|f|\le1$ almost surely.
The argument for $g$ is identical.

We have
\[c_d(f_n,g_n) = \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[(\Pi_d f_n)(\Pi_d g_n)] \underset{n \to\infty}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[(\Pi_d f)(\Pi_d g)] = c_d(f,g)
\]
Thus every sequence in $\mathcal{B}$ has a coordinatewise convergent subsequence.
Since the coordinatewise topology is metrizable, sequential compactness implies $\mathcal{B}$ is (topologically) compact.

We now prove
$\mathcal B\subseteq\overline{\mathcal C}$.
Fix odd $(f,g), |f|,|g| \leq 1$, and put
\[
 f^{(D)}=\sum_{d\le D}\Pi_df,\qquad
 g^{(D)}=\sum_{d\le D}\Pi_dg,\qquad
 \varepsilon_D=
 \|f-f^{(D)}\|_2+\|g-g^{(D)}\|_2.
\]
Then $\varepsilon_D\to0$ as $D \to \infty$.
\cref{thm:closure} (ii) gives odd finite-dimensional
polynomials $F_n,G_n$ of degree at most $D$ such that, also with convergence of all mixed moments,
\[
 (\Pi_dF_n,\Pi_dG_n)_{d\le D}
 \xrightarrow{d}
 (\Pi_df,\Pi_dg)_{d\le D}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 c(F_n,G_n)\longrightarrow c(f^{(D)},g^{(D)})
 \quad\text{in }\ell_1,
 \qquad
 \|F_n\|_2\to\|f^{(D)}\|_2\le1,
\]
and similarly for $G_n$.

Let $\chi(u)=\max\{-1,\min\{u,1\}\}$ be the clipping function to $[-1,1]$.
Convergence in distribution and uniformly bounded fourth
moments imply
 \begin{align}\label{eq:clip1}
 \|F_n-\chi(F_n)\|_2
 &\longrightarrow
 \|f^{(D)}-\chi(f^{(D)})\|_2
 \leq\|f^{(D)}-f\|_2,\\ \notag
 \|G_n-\chi(G_n)\|_2
 &\longrightarrow
 \|g^{(D)}-\chi(g^{(D)})\|_2
 \leq\|g^{(D)}-g\|_2.
 \end{align}
The right inequalities use that clipping is the pointwise projection onto $[-1,1]$.
Orthogonality and Cauchy--Schwarz give the general continuity relations,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coefficient-continuity}
 \begin{aligned}
 \|c(f,g)\|_1&\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2,\\
 \|c(f,g)-c(f',g')\|_1
 &\le\|f-f'\|_2\|g\|_2+\|f'\|_2\|g-g'\|_2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}


Using \cref{eq:clip1} and \eqref{eq:coefficient-continuity}, we obtain
\[
 \limsup_{n \to \infty}
 \|c(\chi(F_n),\chi(G_n))-c(f,g)\|_1
 \le2\varepsilon_D.
\]
The clipped functions are bounded by 1, odd, and finite-dimensional,
so their coefficient sequences belong to $\mathcal C$ by
the sentence after \eqref{eq:odd-threshold-rounding}. Letting $D\to\infty$
proves the inclusion.

It remains to pass from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{K}$.
The set $\mathcal K$ is exactly the set of barycenters of
probability measures on $\mathcal B$.
Indeed, if $c(\mu) \in \mathcal{K}$, then $c(\mu) = \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{(f,g) \sim \mu}c(f,g)$
is also a mixture of elements $c(f,g) \in \mathcal{B}$.
Conversely, a probability
measure on $\mathcal B$ can be lifted\footnote{
The space of bounded odd pairs is a closed subset of
$\overline{L_2}^{\,2}$, hence Polish. Its coefficient map
onto $\mathcal B$ is continuous by
\eqref{eq:coefficient-continuity}. The Jankov--von Neumann
theorem gives a section measurable for the completion of
the given probability measure, which supplies the lift.}
to a measure $\mu$ on odd pairs $(f,g), |f|,|g| \leq 1$,
and then threshold rounding in \eqref{eq:odd-threshold-rounding} ensures $f,g \in \{\pm1\}$ without changing $c(\mu)$.

Probability measures on the compact metric space
$\mathcal B$ form a compact space for weak convergence.
Their barycenters depend continuously on each coordinate,
so $\mathcal K$ is coordinatewise compact and convex.

The inclusion map $\mathcal B\to\ell_1$ is Borel measurable,
and $\|c\|_1\le1$ on $\mathcal B$, so these barycenters are
also Bochner integrals in $\ell_1$. Since
$\overline{\mathcal C}$ is closed and convex
and contains $\mathcal B$, it contains every such
barycenter. Hence
$\mathcal K\subseteq\overline{\mathcal C}$.
Conversely, $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal K$, and
coordinatewise compactness makes $\mathcal K$ closed
in $\ell_1$. Therefore
$\mathcal K=\overline{\mathcal C}$.

label: lem:maximizers-exist
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:maximizers-exist}
    Let $q \in \ell_\infty$ with $q_{2{m}}=0$ for ${m}\ge0$ and assume $\max\operatorname{supp}(q) = D< \infty$.
    Then
    \[
        {v_\infty}(q) = \max\left\{\sum_{m = 0}^\infty q_m \langle \Pi_m f, \Pi_m g\rangle : f,g \in \overline{L_2}, f(X), g(X) \in \{\pm 1\} \textnormal{ a.s.} \right\}\,.
    \]
    Furthermore, there exist optimizers of the form $f = \operatorname{sign}(p)$ and $g = \operatorname{sign}(r)$
    for $p,r \in \overline{\mathcal{H}}_{\le D}$.

label: eq:asymptotic-payoff
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q=\sum_dq_d\Pi_d$ on $\overline{L_2}$. First we claim (this still holds if $\max \operatorname{supp}(q) = \infty$)
\begin{equation}\label{eq:asymptotic-payoff}
 \operatorname{OPT}(Q)=\sup_{c\in\mathcal B}\langle c,q\rangle=v_\infty(q).
\end{equation}
The first equality follows since taking the odd parts of candidates $f,g$ for $\operatorname{OPT}(Q)$ preserves their value, and $f,g \in [-1,1]$ can be replaced by a distribution of $f,g \in \{\pm 1\}$ using the threshold rounding in \eqref{eq:odd-threshold-rounding}.
For the second equality, the inclusion in
\cref{lem:asymptotic-c} and $\ell_1$-continuity of the pairing
give the upper bound
$\sup_{c \in \mathcal B}\langle c,q\rangle
\le\sup_{c \in \mathcal C}\langle c,q\rangle=v_\infty(q)$.
For the reverse inequality, a sequence of $c(\mu^{(k)}) \in \mathcal{C}$ approaching $v_\infty(q)$
has that $c(\mu^{(k)}) = \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{(f,g) \sim \mu^{(k)}}c(f,g)$ is an average
of $c(f,g) \in \mathcal{B}$,
so the inequality follows.

When $q$ has finite support, the map $c \mapsto \langle c, q \rangle$ is coordinatewise
continuous. Compactness of $\mathcal B$ and
\eqref{eq:asymptotic-payoff} therefore give $c \in \mathcal{B}$ achieving value $v_\infty(q)$.
Then any pair $(f,g), |f|, |g| \leq 1$ corresponding to $c$ achieves the maximum value $v_\infty(q)$.

To see that $f,g$ can be polynomial threshold functions, take two successive best responses:
\[
 p=Qg,\qquad f=\operatorname{sign}(p),\qquad
 r=Qf,\qquad g=\operatorname{sign}(r).
\]
Neither replacement decreases the value, and
\eqref{eq:asymptotic-payoff} says that no Boolean pair can
exceed $v_\infty(q)$. Hence $(f,g)$ is optimal.
Both $p$ and $r$ have graded degree at most $D$.

label: cor:krivine-schemes-exact
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
\medskip
\noindent(i)
Choose $q\in\mathcal Q$ attaining the infimum in
\cref{thm:duality}, so $v_\infty(q)=K_G^{-1}$.
For $Q=\sum_dq_d\Pi_d$,
\eqref{eq:asymptotic-payoff} gives $\operatorname{OPT}(Q)=K_G^{-1}$.
Its operator norm is at most $1$, so $\operatorname{SDP}(Q)\le1$.
The standard SDP construction $f(X) = g(X) = (X_1, \dots, X_n)/\sqrt{X_1^2 + \cdots + X_n^2}$ with $n \to \infty$
shows $\operatorname{SDP}(Q)\ge q_1=1$.
Therefore $\operatorname{SDP}(Q)/\operatorname{OPT}(Q)=K_G$.

\medskip\noindent(ii)
For every finitely supported real sequence $b$ supported
on odd degrees, Grothendieck's inequality gives
\[
 \sup_{c\in\mathcal B}\langle c,b\rangle
 =v_\infty(b)
 \ge\operatorname{OPT}(Q_b)
 \ge K_G^{-1}\operatorname{SDP}(Q_b)
\]
where $Q_b = \sum_m b_m \Pi_m$.
By the standard SDP construction, $\operatorname{SDP}(Q_b) \geq b_1$. Therefore, for all such $b$,
\[
 \sup_{c\in\mathcal B}\langle c,b\rangle\ge K_G^{-1} b_1.
\]
Because $\mathcal K$ is coordinatewise compact and convex,
finite-dimensional separation implies
$K_G^{-1} e_1\in\mathcal K$.
By the definition of $\mathcal K$, there is a distribution
$\mu$ on odd asymptotic Boolean pairs with
$c(\mu)=K_G^{-1}e_1$. Hence $H_\mu(t)=t/K_G$ on $[-1,1]$.

name: One-variable criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
Since ${Q}$
is self-adjoint with odd range, successive replacements of
$f=\operatorname{sign}({Q}g)$ and $g=\operatorname{sign}({Q}f)$ cannot decrease the OPT value.
Use $\operatorname{sign}(z_1)$ wherever the argument vanishes; both responses are
then odd almost everywhere.
Put $h:=(f+g)/2$, $k:=(f-g)/2$; then $h^2+k^2=1$.  

Rotate the domain so that $\Pi_1h(z)$ is a nonnegative multiple of $z_1$.
Then $\|\Pi_1h\|_2=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[z_1h]\le\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|z_1|=\sqrt{2/\pi}$, so
$x:=\sqrt{\pi/2}\|\Pi_1h\|_2\in[0,1]$ and $\Pi_1h=\sqrt{2/\pi}xz_1$.
Choose an interval $I\ni x$ and use its associated parameters.

For each $N$ and independent $U,V\sim\gamma_{n}$, set
$\sigma_r:=f(\cos(r\pi/N)U+\sin(r\pi/N)V)$.
Oddness gives $\sigma_{r+N}=-\sigma_r$.
The correlation identity \cref{eq:correlation} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bnbound}
 \sum_jw_j^{(N)}\sum_{m\text{ odd}}\cos^m(\pi j/N)\|\Pi_m f\|_2^2
 =\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\sum_j
w_j^{(N)}\sigma_r\sigma_{r+j}\right]
\stackrel{\cref{eq:rotation-constant}}{\le}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[B_N]
=B_N.
\end{equation}
All series converge absolutely by Parseval. Average for $f,g$ and sum
over $N$, using $(\|\Pi_m(f)\|_2^2+\|\Pi_m g\|_2^2)/2=\|\Pi_m h\|_2^2+\|\Pi_m k\|_2^2$.
Combining this with
$\langle f,{Q}g\rangle=\sum_mq_m(\|\Pi_m h\|_2^2-\|\Pi_m k\|_2^2)$
and $q_1=1$, $q_m=0$ for $m>21$ from \cref{eq:coefficients}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:payoff-residual}
\begin{aligned}
 \langle f,{Q}g\rangle
 &=\sum_{m\,\rm odd}\Gamma_m(\|\Pi_m h\|_2^2+\|\Pi_m k\|_2^2)+\sum_{m\,\rm odd}\bigl((q_m-\Gamma_m)\|\Pi_m h\|_2^2+(-q_m-\Gamma_m)\|\Pi_m k\|_2^2\bigr)\\
&\stackrel{\cref{eq:bnbound}\wedge\cref{eq:rotation-coefficients}\wedge\cref{eq:residual-weights}\wedge\cref{eq:rotation-tail}}{\le} B+(1-\Gamma_1)\frac2\pi x^2
 +\sum_m\bigl(\alpha_m\|\Pi_m h\|_2^2+\beta_m\|\Pi_m k\|_2^2\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Write the Gaussian coordinates as independent
$S\sim\gamma_1$, $Y\sim\gamma_{{n}-1}$, with $Y$ the empty tuple if ${n}=1$.
Let $M(Y)$ be the feasible moments of $f(\cdot,Y),g(\cdot,Y)$. For
$p=0,1$ and $\eta\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^{{n}-1}$, set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 u_p(Y)&:=h_p(M(Y)),&v_p(Y)&:=k_p(M(Y)),\\
 \widehat u_p(\eta)&:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[u_p(Y)\psi_\eta(Y)],&
 \widehat v_p(\eta)&:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[v_p(Y)\psi_\eta(Y)].
\end{aligned}
\]
The last sum in \cref{eq:payoff-residual} equals
\[
\sum_{\eta}\sum_{p=0}^1[\widehat u_p(\eta)^TD_{p,|\eta|}(\alpha)\widehat u_p(\eta)
+\widehat v_p(\eta)^TD_{p,|\eta|}(\beta)\widehat v_p(\eta)].
\]
Also $(h_1(M(Y)))_0=(M_1(Y)+M_{23}(Y))/2=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_S[Sh(S,Y)]$, so
$\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_Y(h_1(M(Y)))_0=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,x$.
In the Hermite expansion in $Y$, coordinate $j$ of $h_p(M),k_p(M)$ at
index $\eta$ has total degree $2j+p+|\eta|$ in $(S,Y)$.
For $1\le|\eta|\le21$, apply
$D_{p,|\eta|}(\alpha)\preceq H_p+\varepsilon I_{11}$ and
$D_{p,|\eta|}(\beta)\preceq K_p+\varepsilon I_{11}$ from \cref{eq:matrix-comparisons}.
For $|\eta|>21$, both diagonal matrices vanish and $H_p,K_p\succeq0$ by the same equation.
When $\eta=0$ and $p=0$, $D_{0,0}(\alpha)=D_{0,0}(\beta)=0$.
For $\eta=0$ and $p=1$, the last inequality of \cref{eq:matrix-comparisons},
applied to $(z,-1)$, gives the following bounds for
$z=\widehat u_1(0)$ and $z=\widehat v_1(0)$, respectively:
\[
z^TD_{1,0}(\alpha)z
\leq z^TH_1z
-2\ell_h^Tz+c_h+\varepsilon+\varepsilon\|z\|_2^2
,\quad
z^TD_{1,0}(\beta)z
\leq z^TK_1z
-2\ell_k^Tz+c_k+\varepsilon+\varepsilon\|z\|_2^2.
\]
Parseval adds these bounds. The constants cost $c_h+c_k+2\varepsilon$,
and the quadratic errors cost at most
\[
 \varepsilon\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_Y\sum_p(\|h_p(M(Y))\|^2+\|k_p(M(Y))\|^2)
 \le\varepsilon\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}(h^2+k^2)=\varepsilon
\]
by Bessel's inequality. 
Combining these estimates into \cref{eq:payoff-residual} then gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:slice-bound}
 \langle f,{Q}g\rangle\le\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_YF(M(Y))+\Phi(x)
 \stackrel{\cref{eq:one-dimensional}}{\le} C+\Phi(x).
\end{equation}
By \cref{eq:rotation-tail}, $\Phi$ is convex. Since $x\in I$,
$C+\Phi(x)\le C+\max_{\partial I}\Phi\le {v_*}$ by \cref{eq:endpoint}, proving the claim.

body_md:
Define
\[
 F_{\rm tr}(W,X):=F(W,X)\prod_{j=1}^3\mathbf1_{\{|X_j|\le73/10\}},
 \qquad C_{\rm tr}[a,b]:=\sum_{|\alpha|=b}
 \left(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F_{\rm tr}(W,X)\psi_a(W)\psi_\alpha(X)]\right)^2,
\]
and $\operatorname{erfc}(x):=2\pi^{-1/2}\int_x^\infty e^{-t^2}\,dt$.
Choose $\hat C[a,b]$ as in Claim~\ref{head:claim-numerical}.
By Parseval and \cref{head:square-difference},
\begin{equation}\label{head:cutoff}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a,b\ge0}|C_{\rm tr}[a,b]-C[a,b]|
 &\le\|F-F_{\rm tr}\|_2(\|F\|_2+\|F_{\rm tr}\|_2)\\
 &\le2\sqrt{3\operatorname{erfc}(73/(10\sqrt2))}
 <1.858282199124\cdot10^{-6},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
since $\|F_{\rm tr}\|_2\le\|F\|_2=1$ and
\[
 \|F-F_{\rm tr}\|_2^2
 =\Pr\!\left(\max_j|X_j|>73/10\right)
 \le\sum_{j=1}^3\Pr(|X_j|>73/10)
 =3\operatorname{erfc}(73/(10\sqrt2)).
\]
For square-summable real vectors $x,y$,
\begin{equation}\label{head:square-difference}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_j|x_j^2-y_j^2|
 &\le\|x-y\|_2\|x+y\|_2\le\|x-y\|_2(\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)\\
 &\le\|x-y\|_2(2\|x\|_2+\|x-y\|_2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $i\ne14$, set $P_{i,+}(t):=\sum_{m\ge1}|[t^m]P_i(t)|t^m$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{root:coefficient-majorant}
\begin{aligned}
 |[t^m](P_i(t)^a(-t)^b)|&\le[t^m](P_{i,+}(t)^at^b),\\
 \sum_{m\ge0}[t^m](P_{i,+}(t)^at^b)&=P_{i,+}(1)^a\le1,\qquad
 [t^m](P_{i,+}(t)^at^b)=0\quad(m<a+b).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Only $a+b\le681$ contributes through degree $681$, by
\cref{root:coefficient-majorant}. That equation,
\cref{head:joint-plane}, and \cref{head:cutoff} give
\begin{equation}\label{head:head-error}
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{m=1}^{681}\left|[t^m]
 \sum_{i\in\{0,\ldots,13,15,16\}}\lambda_i
 \sum_{a+b\le681}(\hat C[a,b]-C[a,b])P_i(t)^a(-t)^b\right|\\
 &\quad\le\left(\sum_{i\in\{0,\ldots,13,15,16\}}\lambda_i\right)
             \sum_{a+b\le681}|\hat C[a,b]-C[a,b]|\\
 &\quad<\frac{1315400222548137891645}{1351351351351351364726}
 \left(6.078879564946870\cdot10^{-8}+1.858282199124\cdot10^{-6}\right)\\
 &\quad<1.868016346073\cdot10^{-6},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the fraction is the sum of the indicated weights.
For \cref{root:coefficient-majorant}, induction from $P_i^0=P_{i,+}^0=1$
uses
\[
 |[t^m]P_i^a|\le\sum_{{j}=0}^m|[t^{j}]P_i|\,|[t^{m-{j}}]P_i^{a-1}|
 \le[t^m]P_{i,+}^a.
\]
Since $P_{i,+}(0)=0$,
\[
 [t^m]P_{i,+}^a=0\quad(m<a),\qquad
 [t^m](P_{i,+}^at^b)=
 \begin{cases}[t^{m-b}]P_{i,+}^a,&m\ge b,\\0,&m<b.\end{cases}
\]
The coefficient sum equals $P_{i,+}(1)^a\le1$.
The triangle inequality and \cref{head:finite-margin} yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 c_1-\sum_{m=2}^{681}|c_m|
 &>0.56187924796168130219-1.868016346073\cdot10^{-6}\\
 &=0.56187737994533522919>0.5618773799453352.
\end{aligned}
\]

body_md:
\smallskip\noindent\textbf{1. Express the Hermite coefficients as integrals.}
Set $\phi(z):=e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and, for real $s$,
\[
 B_j(s):={\mathrm{i}}^{-j}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(X_1)}\psi_j(X_1)\mathbf1_{\{|X_1|\le73/10\}}],
 \qquad B(s):=(B_j(s))_{j=0}^{681},\quad {\mathrm{i}}^2=-1.
\]
For $a+|\alpha|\le681$ odd,
\begin{equation}\label{head:coefficient-integral}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F_{\rm tr}(W,X)\psi_a(W)\psi_\alpha(X)]
 =\frac{2(-1)^{(a+|\alpha|-1)/2}}{\pi\sqrt{a!}}
       \int_0^\infty e^{-s^2/2}s^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^3B_{\alpha_j}(s)\,ds.
\end{equation}
For even $a+|\alpha|$ the coefficient vanishes by
$F_{\rm tr}(-W,-X)=-F_{\rm tr}(W,X)$ and \cref{root:odd-hermite}.
Reflection gives $\overline{B_j(s)}={\mathrm{i}}^j(-1)^j {\mathrm{i}}^jB_j(s)=B_j(s)$,
and Bessel's inequality gives $\|B(s)\|_2\le1$.
To prove \cref{head:coefficient-integral}, for $a\ge0$ and $v\in\mathbb{R}$ use
\begin{equation}\label{head:smoothed-sign}
\begin{aligned}
 q_a(v)&:=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[{\operatorname{sign}}(W+v)\psi_a(W)]
       =\frac{q_0^{(a)}(v)}{\sqrt{a!}},\qquad
 q_0(v)=2\int_0^v\phi(u)\,du,\\
 q_a^{(l)}(v)&=\frac{2(-1)^{a+l-1}}{\sqrt{a!}}
                  \phi(v)\operatorname{He}_{a+l-1}(v)
        \quad(a,l\ge0,\ a+l\ge1),\\
 q_a(v)&=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{a!}}\int_0^\infty
          e^{-s^2/2}s^{a-1}\Im({\mathrm{i}}^ae^{{\mathrm{i}}sv})\,ds.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Conditioning on $X$ and independence give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F_{\rm tr}\psi_a(W)\psi_\alpha(X)]
 &=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[q_a\!\left(\sum_jr(X_j)\right)
       \psi_\alpha(X)\prod_j\mathbf1_{\{|X_j|\le73/10\}}\right],\\
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[e^{{\mathrm{i}}s\sum_jr(X_j)}\psi_\alpha(X)
       \prod_j\mathbf1_{\{|X_j|\le73/10\}}\right]
 &={\mathrm{i}}^{|\alpha|}\prod_jB_{\alpha_j}(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Fubini follows from $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|\psi_\alpha(X)|\le1$ and the integrability of
$e^{-s^2/2}s^{a-1}$ for $a\ge1$; for $a=0$, use
$|\sin(s\sum_jr(X_j))|/s\le3\sup_{|x|\le73/10}|r(x)|$ when
$\max_j|X_j|\le73/10$.
The first two identities in \cref{head:smoothed-sign} follow from
\[
 (\phi\operatorname{He}_{a-1})'=-\phi\operatorname{He}_a,\qquad
 \frac2{\sqrt{a!}}\int_{-v}^\infty\operatorname{He}_a(u)\phi(u)\,du
 =\frac{2(-1)^{a-1}}{\sqrt{a!}}\phi(v)\operatorname{He}_{a-1}(v)\quad(a\ge1).
\]
For the Fourier identity, both sides at $a=0$ vanish at $v=0$, and
\[
 \frac d{dv}\left(\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2/2}
                 \frac{\sin(sv)}s\,ds\right)
 =\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2/2}\cos(sv)\,ds=2\phi(v).
\]
The bounds $|\sin(sv)|/s\le|v|$ and
$|\partial_v^a(\sin(sv)/s)|\le s^{a-1}$ for $a\ge1$, multiplied by
$e^{-s^2/2}$, are integrable in $s$, locally uniformly for real $v$.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{2. Define the finite approximation $\hat C[a,b]$.}
Construct $\hat C$ by the operations below, with fixed summation orders
and fixed choices of separate or combined multiplication and addition.
Use the same resulting rational array in \cref{head:finite-margin}.
Let $s_\nu,\omega_\nu$, $1\le\nu\le768$, be the 24-point
Gauss--Legendre nodes and weights on each $[k,k+1]$, $0\le k\le31$.
Their weighted sum equals the integral on that interval for every polynomial
of degree at most $47$. Set
\[
 U_{a\nu}:=\omega_\nu e^{-s_\nu^2/2}s_\nu^{a-1}/\sqrt{a!}
 \qquad(0\le a\le681).
\]
In interval arithmetic, each operation encloses the exact values by
rounding the lower endpoint downward and the upper endpoint upward,
at the stated precision.
For $[a,b]\subset[0,73/10]$, set $h:=(b-a)/2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{head:inner-M}
\begin{aligned}
 M:={}&\frac{(100/99)^{681/2}(10000/199)^{1/4}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \exp\left(-\frac{50}{199}\max(0,a-h/4)^2+50(3h/4)^2\right)\\
 &\quad\cdot\exp\left(24h\sum_{k=1}^{15}
 \frac{|r^{(k)}((a+b)/2)|}{(k-1)!}(5h/4)^{k-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Starting with $[0,73/10]$, accept an interval only when its
512-bit interval evaluation proves
$8(b-a)M2^{-64}<10^{-10}(b-a)/(73/5)$; otherwise bisect it.
Use the 32-point
Gauss--Legendre rule, exact for polynomials of degree at most $63$,
on each interval. Index its positive nodes by $j$;
for the node $x$ in $[a,b]$, define
\[
 v_j:=2\phi(x)(\psi_m(x))_{m=0}^{681}
 \int_a^b\prod_{\substack{y\ne x\\y\text{ a quadrature node in }[a,b]}}
               \frac{t-y}{x-y}\,dt.
\]
The integral is the quadrature weight. Reflection supplies the factor two:
${\mathrm{i}}^{-m}(e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(x)}+(-1)^me^{-{\mathrm{i}}sr(x)})=2\Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(x)})$.
At $512$ bits, enclose the exact quadrature nodes
and use these enclosures to compute $v_j$, $U_{a\nu}$, $4/\pi^2$, and
$\Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}s_\nu r(x)})$. Round the midpoint of each resulting
enclosure to the nearest IEEE 754 binary64 number, which has at most
$53$ significant binary digits; at a tie, choose the number whose last
stored binary digit is zero. Bound its conversion error against the
whole enclosure. Hats denote computed values whose stored real and
imaginary components are interpreted as exact rationals.
Rounding an exact real result $x$ to the nearest binary64 number has
absolute error at most $2^{-53}|x|+2^{-1074}$, provided that $x$ is
within the representable range.
Compute $\hat B_{\nu m}$ by summing the products of $(\hat v_j)_m$
with the stored values of $\Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}s_\nu r(x)})$, using at most
one multiplication and one addition per term. Round each operation,
or round a multiplication and its following addition together. Write
$\hat B_{\nu\cdot}:=(\hat B_{\nu m})_{m=0}^{681}$.
Let $\hat U_{a\nu}$ denote the conversion before omitting entries
below $10^{-18}$, and, for each
$(\nu,\mu)$, set $g(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{681}\hat B_{\nu j}\hat B_{\mu j}z^j$
with exact products. For odd $a+b\le681$, compute $\hat C[a,b]$ from
\begin{equation}\label{head:computed-sum}
 {\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}
 \sum_{\mu:\hat U_{a\mu}\ge10^{-18}}\hat U_{a\mu}
 \left(\sum_{\nu:\hat U_{a\nu}\ge10^{-18}}\hat U_{a\nu}[z^b]
 \left(\sum_{j=0}^{681}\hat B_{\nu j}\hat B_{\mu j}z^j\right)^3\right).
\end{equation}
Round the products defining $g$ and append zeros to obtain $2048$ entries.
The exact formula approximated by the forward transform, two multiplications
for each cube, and the inverse transform is
\begin{equation}\label{head:discrete-transform}
 [z^b]g(z)^3=\frac1{2048}\sum_{k=0}^{2047}
  g(e^{-2\pi {\mathrm{i}}k/2048})^3e^{2\pi {\mathrm{i}}kb/2048}\quad(0\le b\le2043),
\end{equation}
since $\deg(g^3)\le2043$. First reverse the eleven binary digits of
the indices $0,\ldots,2047$. For $k=1,\ldots,11$, split each consecutive
block of $2^k$ entries into halves and pair their $j$th entries,
$0\le j<2^{k-1}$, applying $(a,b)\mapsto(a+wb,a-wb)$ with
$w=e^{-2\pi {\mathrm{i}}j/2^k}$. Obtain $\hat w$ by rounding the real and imaginary
parts of $w$ from their 256-bit enclosure midpoints, with error $<2^{-48}$
against each enclosure.
The inverse conjugates these roots and ends with division by $2048$.
Take real parts, sum first over $\nu$ and then over $\mu$ in
\cref{head:computed-sum}, and multiply by ${\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}$ with the
same rounding convention; replace negative results
by zero and set $\hat C[a,b]=0$ when $a+b$ is even.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{3. Bound the error in $\hat C$.}
For $s>0$ and real vectors $v,w$ of equal dimension,
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^{681}e^{-s^2}s^{2a-2}/a!\le s^{-2},\qquad
 \|v^{\otimes3}-w^{\otimes3}\|_2
 \le3\|v-w\|_2\max(\|v\|_2,\|w\|_2)^2.
\]
Together with $\|B(s)\|_2\le1$, the 512-bit bound
$\sum_{\nu=1}^{768}\omega_\nu/s_\nu<11.017652258306741$, and
Claim~\ref{head:claim-quadrature}, these inequalities give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left\|\left(
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F_{\rm tr}\psi_a(W)\psi_\alpha(X)]
 -\frac{2(-1)^{(a+|\alpha|-1)/2}}\pi
       \sum_{\nu=1}^{768}U_{a\nu}\prod_{j=1}^3\hat B_{\nu\alpha_j}
 \right)_{\substack{a+|\alpha|\le681\\a+|\alpha|\ \mathrm{odd}}}\right\|_2\\
 &\quad\le2.917598329143\cdot10^{-10}+8.228746\cdot10^{-18}\\
 &\qquad+\frac6\pi\sum_{\nu=1}^{768}\frac{\omega_\nu}{s_\nu}
 (5.604655228362\cdot10^{-12})(1+5.604655228362\cdot10^{-12})^2\\
 &\quad<4.096939258130\cdot10^{-10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $\|F_{\rm tr}\|_2\le1$, \cref{head:square-difference} yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{\substack{a+b\le681\\a+b\ \mathrm{odd}}}\left|
 C_{\rm tr}[a,b]-\frac4{\pi^2}\sum_{|\alpha|=b}
 \left(\sum_{\nu=1}^{768}U_{a\nu}
             \prod_{j=1}^3\hat B_{\nu\alpha_j}\right)^2\right|\\
 &\quad<2(4.096939258130\cdot10^{-10})
             +(4.096939258130\cdot10^{-10})^2<8.193878518\cdot10^{-10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\begin{equation}\label{head:nonnegative-squares}
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{|\alpha|=b}\left(\sum_{\nu=1}^{768}U_{a\nu}
                      \prod_{j=1}^3\hat B_{\nu\alpha_j}\right)^2\\
 &\quad=\sum_{\nu,\mu=1}^{768}U_{a\nu}U_{a\mu}[z^b]
       \left(\sum_{j=0}^{681}\hat B_{\nu j}\hat B_{\mu j}z^j\right)^3.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus Claim~\ref{head:claim-arithmetic} proves \cref{head:joint-plane}:
\[
 \sum_{a+b\le681}|\hat C[a,b]-C_{\rm tr}[a,b]|
 \le8.193878518\cdot10^{-10}+5.996940779766870\cdot10^{-8}
 =6.078879564946870\cdot10^{-8}.
\]

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{4. Evaluate the finite coefficient inequality.}
For $1\le m\le681$, \cref{eq:upper-staircase-kernel} and \cref{root:linear} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 [t^m]H_{14}(t)&=\sum_{\substack{a,b\ge0\\3a+5b=m}}(-1)^a\frac{u_{ab}^2}{a!b!},\\
 [t^m]H_i(t)&=\frac2\pi\sum_{k=0}^{340}
 \frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{4^k(2k+1)}[t^m]P_i(t)^{2k+1}
 \qquad(17\le i\le31),
\end{aligned}
\]
where $u_{ab}$ is defined in \cref{other:staircase-moments} and
$\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F_*(X_1,X_2)\psi_a(X_1)\psi_b(X_2)]=u_{ab}/\sqrt{a!b!}$.
To evaluate $u_{ab}$, define $J_j(x):=\int_x^\infty\operatorname{He}_j(t)\phi(t)\,dt$ and use
\begin{equation}\label{head:hermite-integrals}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_x^y\psi_j(t)\phi(t)\,dt
 &=\frac{J_j(x)-J_j(y)}{\sqrt{j!}}
 &&(-\infty\le x<y\le\infty),\\
 J_0(x)&=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(x/\sqrt2),&
 J_j(x)&=\phi(x)\operatorname{He}_{j-1}(x)\quad(j\ge1),\\
 J_j(-\infty)&=\mathbf1_{\{j=0\}},&J_j(+\infty)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These identities are proved in Claim~\ref{other:claim-staircase}; evaluate them
at $384$ bits on the coordinate intervals of the rectangles where $F_*$ is constant.
For the remaining polynomial arithmetic, retain only degrees through 681:
$P_i(0)=0$ implies $[t^m]P_i^{2k+1}=0$ for $m\le681$, $k>340$, and
products of nonnegative powers cannot lower degree.
Interval evaluation at $256$ bits, using the rational $\hat C[a,b]$, bounds the
first term in \cref{head:finite-margin} below by
$0.561894649254995327808$ and the subtracted sum above by
$1.540129331402561534750\cdot10^{-5}$. Hence
\[
 0.561894649254995327808-1.540129331402561534750\cdot10^{-5}
 >0.56187924796168130219.
\]

body_md:
For an interval $[a,b]$ of length $\ell$, consider the ellipse
\[
 z=\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{4}
       (2e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}+2^{-1}e^{-{\mathrm{i}}\theta}),\qquad0\le\theta\le2\pi.
\]
If the integrand is analytic inside and on this ellipse and has norm
at most $M$ there, the $n$-point Gauss--Legendre error is at most
\begin{equation}\label{head:gauss-error}
 \frac\ell2\frac{64M}{15(1-2^{-2})2^{2n}}
 =\frac{128}{45}\ell M2^{-2n}\le8\ell M2^{-2n}.
\end{equation}
The scalar bound is \cite[Theorem~2.1]{HaleTrefethen2008}.
For complex Euclidean or Gaussian ${L_2}$ spaces, apply it after bounded
complex-linear functionals $v$ and use
$\|x\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|v(x)|$, with
$\|v\|:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|v(x)|$.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{The outer quadrature.}
Apply \cref{head:gauss-error} in Gaussian ${L_2}$ to
\[
 s\longmapsto\frac2\pi\frac{\sin(s(W+\sum_{j=1}^3r(X_j)))}s
                  \prod_{j=1}^3\mathbf1_{\{|X_j|\le73/10\}}.
\]
Its singularity at zero is removable. Since $r$ is bounded on
$[-73/10,73/10]$ and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} e^{s|W|}<\infty$ for every real $s$,
the displayed function is analytic in Gaussian ${L_2}$.
On the ellipses for $[k,k+1]$, $|\Im s|\le3/8$,
so $|\sin(sv)/s|=|v\int_0^1\cos(tsv)\,dt|\le|v|e^{3|v|/8}$ for real $v$.
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[e^{3|r(X_1)|/4}\mathbf1_{\{|X_1|\le73/10\}}]&<2.262302379287,\\
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[r(X_1)^2e^{3|r(X_1)|/4}\mathbf1_{\{|X_1|\le73/10\}}]&<2023.738286188,\\
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} e^{3|W|/4}&\le2e^{9/32},\qquad
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} W^2e^{3|W|/4}\le(25/8)e^{9/32}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By Bessel's inequality, retaining the Hermite coefficients with
$a+|\alpha|\le681$ and $a+|\alpha|$ odd cannot increase the ${L_2}$ norm.
Independence and Minkowski's inequality therefore bound the contribution
of the quadrature on $[0,32]$ to \cref{head:outer-error} by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &8\cdot32\cdot2^{-48}\frac{2\sqrt2}{\pi}e^{9/64}
 \left(\frac54(2.262302379287)^{3/2}
       +3\sqrt{2023.738286188}\,(2.262302379287)\right)\\
 &\qquad<2.917598329143\cdot10^{-10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the first two moments, partition $[0,73/10]$ into intervals of length
$10^{-3}$. On each $[a,b]$, let $R$ be the upper endpoint of the modulus
of the 512-bit interval polynomial evaluation $r([a,b])$ and sum
\[
\begin{aligned}
 2\int_a^b e^{3|r(x)|/4}\phi(x)\,dx&\le2(b-a)\phi(a)e^{3R/4},\\
 2\int_a^b r(x)^2e^{3|r(x)|/4}\phi(x)\,dx&\le2(b-a)\phi(a)R^2e^{3R/4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor two uses oddness of $r$ and evenness of $\phi$.
For $s\ge32$, Bessel's inequality and a geometric sum give
\[
 \sum_{|\alpha|\le681-a}\left|\prod_jB_{\alpha_j}(s)\right|^2\le1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{a=0}^{681}\frac{s^{2a}}{a!}
 \le\frac{s^{1362}}{681!}\sum_{j=0}^{681}(681/s^2)^j
 \le\frac{1024s^{1362}}{343\cdot681!}.
\]
Minkowski's inequality bounds the integral over $s>32$ by
\begin{equation}\label{head:fourier-tail}
\begin{aligned}
 &\left\|\left(\frac2{\pi\sqrt{a!}}\int_{32}^\infty
 e^{-s^2/2}s^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^3B_{\alpha_j}(s)\,ds
 \right)_{\substack{a+|\alpha|\le681\\a+|\alpha|\ \text{odd}}}\right\|_2\\
 &\quad\le\frac{64}{\pi\sqrt{343\cdot681!}}
              \int_{32}^\infty e^{-s^2/2}s^{680}\,ds
 \le\frac{64e^{-512}32^{681}}{345\pi\sqrt{343\cdot681!}}
 <3\cdot10^{-18}<8.228746\cdot10^{-18}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The second inequality follows by integrating
\[
 -\frac d{ds}(e^{-s^2/2}s^{679})
 =e^{-s^2/2}s^{680}(1-679/s^2)
 \ge\frac{345}{1024}e^{-s^2/2}s^{680}\quad(s\ge32).
\]

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{The computation of $\hat B$.}
On the ellipse over $[a,b]$, $|z-(a+b)/2|\le5h/4$,
$|\Im z|\le3h/4$, and $|\Re z|\ge\max(0,a-h/4)$.
Mehler's identity and the Taylor expansion of $r$ give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j=0}^{681}|\psi_j(z)|^2
 &\le(100/99)^{681}\sum_{j\ge0}(99/100)^j|\psi_j(z)|^2\\
 &=(100/99)^{681}(10000/199)^{1/2}
   e^{(99/199)(\Re z)^2+99(\Im z)^2},\\
 |\Im r(z)|&\le|\Im z|\sum_{k=1}^{15}
 \frac{|r^{(k)}((a+b)/2)|}{(k-1)!}|z-(a+b)/2|^{k-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying the square root of the first bound by
$|\phi(z)e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(z)}|\le(2\pi)^{-1/2}
 e^{-(\Re z)^2/2+(\Im z)^2/2+32|\Im r(z)|}$ yields
$\|(\phi(z)\psi_j(z)e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(z)})_{j=0}^{681}\|_2\le M$ for $0\le s\le32$,
with $M$ as in \cref{head:inner-M}. The bisection accepts 50 intervals,
giving 1600 positive nodes and
\begin{equation}\label{head:inner-total}
 2\sum_{[a,b]}8(b-a)M2^{-64}<3.288380170604\cdot10^{-12}.
\end{equation}
The sum is over the accepted intervals. By reflection and
\cref{head:gauss-error}, it bounds
\[
 \left\|B(s)-\left(\sum_x(v_j)_m
       \Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}sr(x)})\right)_{m=0}^{681}\right\|_2
 \quad(0\le s\le32),
\]
where $j$ indexes $x$ as in step 2.
Put $\gamma_k:=k2^{-53}/(1-k2^{-53})$ for integers $0\le k<2^{53}$.
For an $n$-term dot product, $2n<2^{53}$, using at most $n$
multiplications and $n$ additions with the stated rounding and no overflow,
the error is at most $\gamma_{2n}$ times the sum of the absolute
values of its summands, apart from the additive $2^{-1074}$ rounding errors.
Rounding a multiplication and addition together does not increase this bound.
For every quadrature node and $0\le m\le681$, the input enclosures verify
\[
 \left|\widehat{\Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}s_\nu r(x)})}
             -\Re({\mathrm{i}}^{-m}e^{{\mathrm{i}}s_\nu r(x)})\right|<2^{-48}.
\]
The same 512-bit evaluation gives
\[
 \sum_j\|v_j-\hat v_j\|_2<3.050177189723512\cdot10^{-16},
 \qquad \sum_j\|v_j\|_2<6.454332802795005.
\]
\begin{align}
 \|\hat B_{\nu\cdot}-B(s_\nu)\|_2
 \le{}&3.288380170604\cdot10^{-12}+\sum_j\|v_j-\hat v_j\|_2\notag\\
 &+(2^{-48}+\gamma_{3200}(1+2^{-48}))
       \sum_j(\|v_j\|_2+\|v_j-\hat v_j\|_2)+10^{-290}\notag\\
 &<5.604655228362\cdot10^{-12}.\label{head:B-error-detail}
\end{align}

body_md:
For each $(\nu,\mu)$, Cauchy--Schwarz and \cref{head:B-error} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|&\le\|\hat B_{\nu\cdot}\|_2\|\hat B_{\mu\cdot}\|_2
 \le(1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^2,\\
 \sum_j|[z^j]g(z)^3|&\le\left(\sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|\right)^3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here and below the weight indices range over $0\le a\le681$,
$1\le\nu,\mu\le768$.
The input enclosures and stored numbers give, at $256$ bits,
\begin{equation}\label{head:input-totals}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a,\nu}|U_{a\nu}-\hat U_{a\nu}|&<1.092870488954584\cdot10^{-15},&
 \sum_{a,\nu}|\hat U_{a\nu}|&<26.904610216896492,\\
 \sum_a\left(\sum_\nu|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2&<61.515376731920361,&
 \left|\frac4{\pi^2}-{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}\right|&<1.586515951775777\cdot10^{-17},\\
 \sum_{a,\nu:\hat U_{a\nu}<10^{-18}}|\hat U_{a\nu}|&<2.655682807169783\cdot10^{-15},&
 {\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}&=\frac{228155022448185}{562949953421312}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For conversion of the weights and $4/\pi^2$,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{a=0}^{681}\sum_{\nu,\mu=1}^{768}
 \left|\frac4{\pi^2}U_{a\nu}U_{a\mu}
       -{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}\hat U_{a\nu}\hat U_{a\mu}\right|
 &\le\frac4{\pi^2}
 \left(\sum_{a,\nu}|U_{a\nu}-\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)
 \left(2\sum_{a,\nu}|\hat U_{a\nu}|+
              \sum_{a,\nu}|U_{a\nu}-\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)\notag\\
 &\quad+\left|\frac4{\pi^2}-{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}\right|
       \sum_a\left(\sum_\nu|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2\notag\\
 &<8.386939012631\cdot10^{-14}.\label{head:U-error}
\end{align}
Multiplication by
$(1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^6$ bounds the resulting coefficient error.
Omitting entries below $10^{-18}$ contributes at most
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}(1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^6
 \sum_a\sum_{\substack{\nu,\mu\\
       \hat U_{a\nu}<10^{-18}\ \mathrm{or}\ \hat U_{a\mu}<10^{-18}}}
            |\hat U_{a\nu}\hat U_{a\mu}|\\
 &\quad\le{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}(1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^6
 \sum_a\left[2\left(\sum_\nu|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)
 \left(\sum_{\nu:\hat U_{a\nu}<10^{-18}}|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)
 +\left(\sum_{\nu:\hat U_{a\nu}<10^{-18}}|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2\right]\\
 &\quad<5.791527838\cdot10^{-14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In each transform in \cref{head:discrete-transform}, the eleven
stages $(a,b)\mapsto(a+wb,a-wb)$ satisfy
\[
 |a+wb|^2+|a-wb|^2=2(|a|^2+|b|^2)\quad(|w|=1).
\]
For $a,b\in\mathbb{C}$, let $\widehat{ab}$ be their product computed with four
real multiplications and two real additions. Apart from the additive
$2^{-1074}$ errors treated below,
\[
 |\widehat{ab}-ab|
 \le\sqrt2(2\cdot2^{-53}+2^{-106})|a||b|\le3\cdot2^{-53}|a||b|.
\]
The component errors in $w$ therefore give
\[
 |\widehat{\hat w b}-wb|
 \le\bigl(\sqrt2\,2^{-48}+3\cdot2^{-53}(1+\sqrt2\,2^{-48})\bigr)|b|
 \le50\cdot2^{-53}|b|.
\]
The two final additions give stage error at most
$(51+50\cdot2^{-53})2^{-53}\sqrt{2(|a|^2+|b|^2)}$,
where $51+50\cdot2^{-53}<100$.
For $0\le k\le11$, $(1+100\cdot2^{-53})^k-1\le\gamma_{100k}$.
Including rounded input products, the Euclidean error after $k$ stages is at most
\[
 2^{k/2}(\gamma_{100k}(1+2^{-53})+2^{-53})
       \sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|
 \le5.53175\cdot10^{-12}\sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|.
\]
In exact arithmetic, each intermediate entry is a sum of distinct input
coefficients with multipliers of modulus one, so its modulus is at most
$\sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|$.
For coordinatewise cubes of complex vectors,
\[
 \|v^3-w^3\|_2\le3\max(\|v\|_\infty,\|w\|_\infty)^2\|v-w\|_2.
\]
For $(zz)z$, the product bound gives rounding error at most
$((1+3\cdot2^{-53})^2-1)|z|^3\le\gamma_{20}|z|^3$.
For the computed forward-transform vector $v\in\mathbb{C}^{2048}$, rounding
these cubes contributes Euclidean error at most
$\gamma_{20}\sqrt{2048}\|v\|_\infty^3$.
The Euclidean operator norm
of the inverse transform is $1/\sqrt{2048}$, and
$\|v\|_1\le\sqrt{2048}\|v\|_2$. The sum of absolute coefficient
errors is therefore at most
\begin{align}
 \left(\sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|\right)^3\bigl(&3(1+5.53175\cdot10^{-12})^2
                                     (5.53175\cdot10^{-12})\notag\\
 &+\sqrt{2048}(\gamma_{20}+\gamma_{1100}(1+\gamma_{20}))
                  (1+5.53175\cdot10^{-12})^3\bigr)
 <2.222247\cdot10^{-11}\label{head:fft-derived}
\end{align}
and, including the additive rounding errors, at most
\begin{equation}\label{head:fft-allocated}
 10000\cdot2048\cdot2^{-53}\left(\sum_j|[z^j]g(z)|\right)^3+10^{-290}
 <2.273736754509\cdot10^{-9}.
\end{equation}
For each $(\nu,\mu)$, the input products, two transforms, cubes, and
inverse normalization use at most
\[
 682+22\cdot1024\cdot10+2048(12+2)<2^{22}
\]
real operations. The bounds for $0\le k\le11$ give forward values of modulus at most
\[
 (1+5.53175\cdot10^{-12})(1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^2
 +4\cdot2^{22}\cdot2^{11}\cdot2^{-1074}<\frac32.
\]
An error in a real product passes through at most two remaining real
additions and is copied to the two outputs, with Euclidean amplification
$\sqrt2(1+2^{-53})^2<4$. With local rounding errors separated, each
remaining linear stage map has operator norm $<2$.
The forward and cube bounds give inverse inputs of
modulus $<8$, and all inverse intermediate magnitudes are bounded by
\[
 8\cdot2048(1+100\cdot2^{-53})^{11}
 +4\cdot2^{22}\cdot2^{11}\cdot2^{-1074}<2^{15}<2^{16}.
\]
Thus the transform and cube operations do not overflow.
With the relative rounding factors fixed, each computed product is
bilinear over $\mathbb{R}$, and the product bound gives input-error amplification at most
\[
 3(1+3\cdot2^{-53})^2\left(\frac32\right)^2<12
 \qquad(|z|<3/2)
\]
for the two products forming $z^3$.
Errors within these multiplications have amplification at most $4\cdot12$.
Across at most $22$ transform stages and the final
division by $2048$, a local error contributes at most
\[
 4\cdot2^{22}\cdot12\cdot\frac{\sqrt{2048}}{2048}
 <2^{24}<2^{40}
\]
times its magnitude to the sum of absolute coefficient errors.
Errors in the final division have amplification one. The total additive
error is $<2^{22}2^{-1074}2^{40}<10^{-300}$.
All $B$ dot products and weighted sums together use fewer than
$2\cdot1600\cdot768\cdot682+682^2(2\cdot768^2+8\cdot768)<2^{40}$
operations. Their intermediate magnitudes are bounded, respectively, by
$2\sum_j(\|v_j\|_2+\|v_j-\hat v_j\|_2)<16$ and
$2(1+\sum_{a,\nu}|\hat U_{a\nu}|)^2<2^{12}$, so they do not overflow.
A local error reaches its dot-product or weighted-sum output through at
most two weight multiplications, the final factor, and $1185792$ rounded
operations. Its amplification is at most
\[
 (1+2^{-53})^{1185792}\max\!\left(1,{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}\right)
 \left(1+\sum_{a,\nu}|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2<2^{12}.
\]
Their additive errors therefore sum to less than
$2^{40}2^{12}2^{-1074}<10^{-300}<10^{-290}$.
Taking real parts cannot increase error, since $|\Re z|\le|z|$.
Using \cref{head:U-error} with the larger coefficient bound from
\cref{head:fft-allocated}, the conversion error is at most
\[
 (8.386939012631\cdot10^{-14})
 ((1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^6+2.273736754509\cdot10^{-9})
 <8.386939032\cdot10^{-14}.
\]
After multiplication by the weights, the error in the computed cube
coefficients and the error in the final sums are respectively bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}\sum_a\left(\sum_\nu|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2
 (2.273736754509\cdot10^{-9})<5.668708385\cdot10^{-8},\\
 &\gamma_{1185792}{\widehat{\frac4{\pi^2}}}
 \sum_a\left(\sum_\nu|\hat U_{a\nu}|\right)^2
 ((1+5.604656\cdot10^{-12})^6+2.273736754509\cdot10^{-9})
 +10^{-290}\\
 &\qquad<3.282182163\cdot10^{-9},
\end{aligned}
\]
The inner sums, outer sum, and final multiplication use at most
$768(2\cdot768)+2\cdot768+1\le2\cdot768^2+8\cdot768=1185792$
real operations per coefficient. Adding the conversion, omission,
transform, and summation bounds gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
 &8.386939032\cdot10^{-14}+5.791527838\cdot10^{-14}
 +5.668708385\cdot10^{-8}+3.282182163\cdot10^{-9}\\
 &\qquad=5.996940779766870\cdot10^{-8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The exact entries are nonnegative by \cref{head:nonnegative-squares};
$|\max(x,0)-y|\le|x-y|$ for $y\ge0$ shows that replacing negative
entries by zero cannot increase error.

body_md:
For $17\le i\le31$, \cref{root:linear},
\cref{root:coefficient-majorant}, and
\begin{equation}\label{other:arcsin-series}
 \arcsin z=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{4^k(2k+1)}z^{2k+1}
 \qquad(|z|\le1)
\end{equation}
give
\[
 |[t^m]H_i(t)|\le[t^m]\frac2\pi\arcsin P_{i,+}(t),\qquad
 \sum_{m\ge0}[t^m]\frac2\pi\arcsin P_{i,+}(t)
 =\frac2\pi\arcsin P_{i,+}(1)\le1.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{other:positive-arcsine-tail}
 \sum_{m>681}|[t^m]H_i(t)|
 \le1-\sum_{m=1}^{681}[t^m]\frac2\pi\arcsin P_{i,+}(t).
\end{equation}
For $19\le i\le31$, evaluate at $256$ bits the finite sum
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{m=1}^{681}[t^m]\frac2\pi\arcsin P_{i,+}(t)
 &=\frac2\pi\sum_{k=0}^{340}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{4^k(2k+1)}
            \sum_{m=1}^{681}[t^m]P_{i,+}(t)^{2k+1},\\
 [t^m]P_{i,+}^{2k+1}&=0\quad(m<2k+1).
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $i=17,18$, set
\[
 \alpha:=[t]P_i>0,\qquad\beta:=-[t^3]P_i>0,\qquad
 (R,\eta):=\begin{cases}(6/5,19/20),&i=17,\\
                         (21/20,49/50),&i=18.
             \end{cases}
\]
For $z=Re^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}$ and $x=\cos\theta$,
\[
 \Re P_i(z)=(\alpha R+3\beta R^3)x-4\beta R^3x^3.
\]
Its squared endpoint and interior critical values satisfy
\[
 (\alpha R-\beta R^3)^2<\eta^2,\qquad
 \frac{(\alpha R+3\beta R^3)^3}{27\beta R^3}<\eta^2
 \quad\text{if }\frac{\alpha R+3\beta R^3}{12\beta R^3}<1.
\]
Thus $\sup_{|z|\le R}|\Re P_i(z)|<\eta$ by the maximum principle.
On $|\Re w|<1$, take the analytic branch of $\arcsin$ with
$\arcsin(0)=0$, $\arcsin'(0)=1$. For $w=x+{\mathrm{i}}y$, $|x|\le\eta$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |1-w^2|^2&=(1-x^2)^2+2(1+x^2)y^2+y^4\ge(1-\eta^2)^2,\\
 |\arcsin w|&=\left|\int_0^1\frac{w}{\sqrt{1-t^2w^2}}\,dt\right|
                 \le\frac{|w|}{\sqrt{1-\eta^2}}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Cauchy's estimate and oddness give
\[
 |[t^m]H_i(t)|\le
 \frac{2(\alpha R+\beta R^3)}{\pi\sqrt{1-\eta^2}}R^{-m},
 \qquad[t^{2m}]H_i(t)=0,
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{other:cubic-tail}
 \sum_{m>681}|[t^m]H_i(t)|
 \le\frac{2(\alpha R+\beta R^3)}{\pi\sqrt{1-\eta^2}}
                         \frac{R^{-683}}{1-R^{-2}}
 <\begin{cases}6.982\cdot10^{-54},&i=17,\\
               1.223\cdot10^{-13},&i=18.
   \end{cases}
\end{equation}
These calculations use the normalized coefficients
\cref{root:normalization}. Summing the $256$-bit interval bounds
\cref{other:positive-arcsine-tail} and \cref{other:cubic-tail}
with weights $\lambda_i$ gives \cref{other:hyperplane-numeric}.

We use the inequalities
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:profile-checks}
 r(27/4)>7,\qquad r^{(j)}(27/4)>0\quad(1\le j\le15),\qquad
 |r(x)|<33/20\quad(|x|\le7/2).
\end{equation}
For $s\ge0$, \cref{heavy:cap-definition} and
$0\le\chi(u)\le1$ for $0\le u\le1$ give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r'(27/4+s)&=\sum_{j=1}^{15}\frac{r^{(j)}(27/4)}{(j-1)!}s^{j-1}>0,\\
 \min\{r(27/4+s),\widetilde r(27/4+s)\}&\ge r(27/4)>7.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \max_j|X_j|\le27/4&\implies F=\widetilde F,\\
 |X_i|>27/4,\quad\max_{j\ne i}|X_j|\le7/2,\quad |W|\le37/10
 &\implies F=\widetilde F={\operatorname{sign}}(X_i),
 \end{aligned}
\]
because $7=2(33/20)+37/10$. Hence
\[
 \{F\ne\widetilde F\}\subseteq
 \bigcup_{i\ne j}\{|X_i|>27/4,\ |X_j|>7/2\}
 \cup\bigcup_i\{|X_i|>27/4,\ |W|>37/10\},
 \qquad 1\le i,j\le3.
\]
Independence and the union bound give
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:disagreement-bound}
 {\Pr}(F\ne\widetilde F)
 \le6\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{27}{4\sqrt2}\right)
 \operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac7{2\sqrt2}\right)
 +3\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{27}{4\sqrt2}\right)
 \operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{37}{10\sqrt2}\right).
\end{equation}
Parseval and \cref{head:square-difference} yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{a\ge0,\,\beta\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^3}
 \left|\bigl(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[F\psi_a(W)\psi_\beta(X)]\bigr)^2
 -\bigl(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[\widetilde F\psi_a(W)\psi_\beta(X)]\bigr)^2\right|\\
 &\qquad\le\|F-\widetilde F\|_2\|F+\widetilde F\|_2
 \le4\sqrt{{\Pr}(F\ne\widetilde F)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Together with \cref{root:coefficient-majorant} and \cref{eq:correlation},
this proves \cref{heavy:weighted-perturbation}; the numerical evaluation
of \cref{heavy:disagreement-bound} uses interval rounding at $256$ bits.

The conclusions
\[
 0\le\chi(u)\le1\quad(0\le u\le1),\qquad
 \widetilde r\in C^6(\mathbb{R})
\]
follow from
\[
 \chi(0)=1,\quad\chi(1)=0,\quad\chi'(u)=-2772u^5(1-u)^5,\quad
 \chi^{(j)}(0)=\chi^{(j)}(1)=0\quad(1\le j\le5).
\]
For $c=-7/2+(2k+1)/32$, $0\le k<112$, the Taylor bounds
\[
 |x-c|\le1/32\implies
 |r(x)|\le|r(c)|+\sum_{j=1}^{15}\frac{|r^{(j)}(c)|}{j!32^j}<33/20
\]
and the values $r(27/4),r^{(j)}(27/4)$, $1\le j\le15$, verify
\cref{heavy:profile-checks} with interval rounding at $256$ bits.
The definition of $\widetilde r$ gives boundedness and vanishing
derivatives outside $[-7,7]$.

title: Proof
body_md:
To bound $|\mathcal D^4\widetilde H_i(t)|$ when $|P_i(t)|<1$, define
\[
 \widetilde C[a,b]:=\sum_{|\beta|=b}
 \bigl(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[\widetilde F(W,X)\psi_a(W)\psi_\beta(X)]\bigr)^2
 \qquad(a,b\ge0).
\]
For $\alpha\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^3$, write
$\alpha!:=\prod_i\alpha_i!$ and
$\partial^\alpha:=\partial_{x_1}^{\alpha_1}\partial_{x_2}^{\alpha_2}
\partial_{x_3}^{\alpha_3}$; $[z^\alpha]$ denotes the coefficient of
$\prod_i z_i^{\alpha_i}$. Derivatives at $X$ are evaluated at $x=X$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:chain-rule}
 B_{\alpha,l}(x):=\frac{\alpha!}{l!}[z^\alpha]
 \left(\sum_{i=1}^3\sum_{h=1}^4
 \frac{\widetilde r^{(h)}(x_i)}{h!}z_i^h\right)^l
 \qquad(1\le l\le|\alpha|\le4).
\end{equation}
For $1\le l\le j\le4$, set
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:T-definition}
 T_{j,l}:=\sum_{|\alpha|=j}\frac{j!}{\alpha!}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[B_{\alpha,l}(X)^2],
 \qquad
 \begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 j\backslash l&1&2&3&4\\\hline
 1&0.099&&&\\
 2&0.221&0.335&&\\
 3&0.36&3.38&4.88&\\
 4&1.11&24.3&124&110
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Use $(n)_0:=1$, $(n)_j:=n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1)$ for $1\le j\le n$,
$(n)_j:=0$ for $j>n\ge0$, and $(-1)!!:=1$.
We set $0^0=1$.
\begin{heavyclaim}\label{heavy:claim-endpoint}
Each entry in \cref{heavy:T-definition} is a strict upper bound for $T_{j,l}$, and
\[
 \widetilde C[a,b]\ge0,\qquad\sum_{a,b}\widetilde C[a,b]=1,\qquad
 \widetilde H_i(t)=\sum_{a,b}\widetilde C[a,b]P_i(t)^a(-t)^b.
\]
This series defines the extension of $\widetilde H_i$ to complex $|t|\le1$.
For nonnegative integers $p,j$ and $0\le\rho<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:M-estimates}
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a\ge p,b\ge0}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}\widetilde C[a,b]
 &\le\frac{2(2p-3)!!}{\pi(1-\rho^2)^{p-1/2}}&&(1\le p\le4),\\
 \sum_{a\ge p,b\ge j}(a)_p(b)_j\rho^{a-p}\widetilde C[a,b]
 &\le\left(\sum_{l=1}^j
 \sqrt{\frac{2T_{j,l}(2p+2l-3)!!}
 {\pi(1-\rho^2)^{p+l-1/2}}}\right)^2&&(j\ge1,\ p+j\le4).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $i\in\{0,15,16\}$, $|t|=1$ and $|P_i(t)|<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:D4-endpoint}
 \begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal D^4\widetilde H_i(t)|\le{}&24
 \sum_{\substack{p,j\ge0\\1\le p+j\le4}}\frac1{p!j!}
 [z^4]\left(\sum_{h=1}^4\frac{|\mathcal D^hP_i(t)|}{h!}z^h\right)^p
 \left(\sum_{h=1}^4\frac{z^h}{h!}\right)^j\\
 &\quad\cdot\sum_{a\ge p,b\ge j}
 (a)_p(b)_j|P_i(t)|^{a-p}\widetilde C[a,b].
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The series and its first four $\mathcal D$-derivatives converge uniformly
on $\{t:|t|\le1,\ |P_i(t)|\le\rho\}$ for every $0\le\rho<1$.
\end{heavyclaim}

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $-1<\Re z<1$, the Gaussian density in coordinates
$u=(x+y)/\sqrt2$, $v=(x-y)/\sqrt2$ continues to
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:complex-density}
 \frac{\exp\bigl(-u^2/(2(1+z))-v^2/(2(1-z))\bigr)}
 {2\pi\sqrt{(1+z)(1-z)}},
\end{equation}
with the analytic square-root branch positive for real $-1<z<1$.
For $t=e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}$, $0<\theta<\pi$, and
$\Re((1\pm P_i(t))^{-1})>0$, multiply the four densities
\cref{heavy:complex-density} at correlations $P_i(t),-t,-t,-t$.
For $\sigma=\pm1$, under the probability law whose density is the
absolute value of this product divided by its integral over $\mathbb{R}^8$, set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Y_{0,\sigma}&:=\Re((1+\sigma P_i(t))^{-1})\frac{(W+\sigma W')^2}{2},\\
 Y_{1,\sigma}&:=\frac14\sum_{j=1}^3(X_j+\sigma X'_j)^2,\qquad
 Y:=(Y_{0,+},Y_{0,-},Y_{1,+},Y_{1,-}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $1\le k\le4$, define
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:ell}
 \begin{aligned}
 \ell_k(Y):=-\frac{k!}{2}[\epsilon^k]\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}\biggl(
 &\ln(1+\sigma P_i(te^\epsilon))+3\ln(1-\sigma te^\epsilon)\\
 &+\frac{Y_{0,\sigma}}
 {\Re((1+\sigma P_i(t))^{-1})(1+\sigma P_i(te^\epsilon))}
 +\frac{2Y_{1,\sigma}}{1-\sigma te^\epsilon}\biggr),
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
holding $Y$ and $\Re((1+\sigma P_i(t))^{-1})$ constant in $\epsilon$.
\begin{heavyclaim}\label{heavy:claim-arc}
For $i\in\{0,15,16\}$ and every compact interval $I\subset(0,\pi)$ with
$\inf_{\theta\in I}\Re((1\pm P_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}))^{-1})>0$,
$\widetilde H_i$ continues analytically to a neighborhood of the arc.
For $\theta\in I$ and $t=e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}$,
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:score-bound}
 |\mathcal D^4\widetilde H_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})|\le
 \frac{(2/\sqrt{2\sin\theta})^3
 \sqrt{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|\ell_1^4+6\ell_1^2\ell_2+3\ell_2^2+4\ell_1\ell_3+\ell_4|^2}}
 {\sqrt{|1-P_i(t)^2|\Re((1+P_i(t))^{-1})\Re((1-P_i(t))^{-1})}}.
\end{equation}
The coordinates of $Y$ are independent, with
\[
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} e^{sY_{0,\sigma}}=(1-2s)^{-1/2},\qquad
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} e^{sY_{1,\sigma}}=(1-2s)^{-3/2}
 \quad(\sigma=\pm1,\ s<1/2).
\]
\end{heavyclaim}

Use the $6284$ closed intervals
\[
 I\in\left\{\left[\frac{k}{4000},\frac{k+1}{4000}\right]:0\le k\le6282\right\}
 \cup\left\{\left[\frac{6283}{4000},\frac\pi2\right]\right\}.
\]
The interval computations specified at the end of this subsection give, for every
$(i,I)$, an upper bound
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in I}|\mathcal D^4\widetilde H_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})|
 \le U_{i,I}<\infty,
\]
with at least one of
Claims~\ref{heavy:claim-endpoint} and~\ref{heavy:claim-arc}
applicable throughout $I$. Before rounding to the displayed decimal
bounds, the interval computations give
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:panel-numerics}
 \begin{aligned}
 \left(\frac2\pi\sum_I|I|
 \left(\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_iU_{i,I}\right)^2\right)^{1/2}
 &<215825.836929,\\
 \frac{\left(\frac2\pi\sum_I|I|
 \left(\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_iU_{i,I}\right)^2\right)^{1/2}}
 {\sqrt{14\cdot681^7}}
 +4\sqrt{{\Pr}(F\ne\widetilde F)}\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_i
 &<0.000007875733380418.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{root:normalization} and Claim~\ref{heavy:claim-endpoint} give
\[
 \sum_{m\ge0}|[t^m]\widetilde H_i|
 \le\sum_{a,b}\widetilde C[a,b]
 \left(\sum_{m\ge1}|[t^m]P_i|\right)^a\le1,
\]
so convergence is uniform on the closed disk. The normalized polynomials
$P_i$ specified by Table~\ref{root:recipe} satisfy
$[t]P_i>0$, $[t^3]P_i<0$, $[t]P_i-[t^3]P_i=1$, whence
\[
 |P_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})|^2
 =1+4([t]P_i)([t^3]P_i)\cos^2\theta<1\quad(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}\ne\pm {\mathrm{i}}),
 \qquad P_i({\mathrm{i}})={\mathrm{i}},\quad\Re((1\pm P_i({\mathrm{i}}))^{-1})=\tfrac12.
\]
Claim~\ref{heavy:claim-endpoint} gives continuous derivatives through
order four away from $\pm {\mathrm{i}}$; Claim~\ref{heavy:claim-arc} and conjugation
give analytic continuation near $\pm {\mathrm{i}}$. Since
\[
 |P_i(t)|\le([t]P_i-[t^3]P_i)|t|=|t|<1\qquad(|t|<1),
\]
the integral against the product Gaussian density is holomorphic on the
open unit disk. It agrees there with the Hermite series by
\cref{eq:correlation} on the real interval and the identity theorem;
the arc integral continues this same function.
Thus $\widetilde H_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})$ is $C^4$ and
$d^4/d\theta^4=({\mathrm{i}}\mathcal D)^4=\mathcal D^4$.
Oddness and real coefficients give
$\widetilde H_i(-t)=-\widetilde H_i(t)$ and
$\widetilde H_i(\bar t)=\overline{\widetilde H_i(t)}$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:panel-sum}
 \begin{aligned}
 \left\|\mathcal D^4\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_i\widetilde H_i
 \right\|_{{L_2}(\mathbb T)}^2
 &=\frac2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}
 \left|\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_i
 \mathcal D^4\widetilde H_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})\right|^2d\theta\\
 &\le\frac2\pi\sum_I|I|
 \left(\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_iU_{i,I}\right)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus \cref{heavy:panel-numerics} gives
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:circle-numerical}
 \left\|\mathcal D^4\sum_{i\in\{0,15,16\}}\lambda_i\widetilde H_i
 \right\|_{{L_2}(\mathbb T)}<215825.836929
\end{equation}
and \cref{heavy:combined-numerical}.

title: Proof
body_md:
\cref{heavy:M-estimates} implies \cref{heavy:D4-endpoint} by
the triangle inequality and the expansions
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal D^4(P_i(t)^a(-t)^b)
 &=24[z^4]P_i(te^z)^a(-t)^be^{bz},\\
 P_i(te^z)^a
 &=\sum_{p=0}^a\frac{(a)_p}{p!}P_i(t)^{a-p}(P_i(te^z)-P_i(t))^p,\\
 P_i(te^z)-P_i(t)&=\sum_{h=1}^4\frac{\mathcal D^hP_i(t)}{h!}z^h+O(z^5),\\
 e^{bz}&=\sum_{j=0}^b\frac{(b)_j}{j!}(e^z-1)^j,\qquad
 \mathcal D^hP_i(t)=([t]P_i)t+3^h([t^3]P_i)t^3.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $|z|\le1$ and $1\le h\le4$,
\[
 |\mathcal D^hP_i(z)|\le[t]P_i-3^h[t^3]P_i.
\]
The expansions and \cref{heavy:M-estimates} therefore give, for
$0\le j\le4$ and $0\le\rho<1$,
\[
 \sum_{a,b}\widetilde C[a,b]
 \sup_{\substack{|z|\le1\\|P_i(z)|\le\rho}}
 \left|\left.\mathcal D^j(P_i(t)^a(-t)^b)\right|_{t=z}\right|<\infty,
\]
proving uniform convergence, in particular near $\pm1$ since
$|P_i(\pm1)|<1$.

To prove \cref{heavy:M-estimates}, conditioning on $X$ gives
\[
 \widetilde C[a,b]=\sum_{|\beta|=b}
 \left(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\left[q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(X_i)\right)
 \psi_\beta(X)\right]\right)^2,
\]
where $q_a$ is defined in \cref{head:smoothed-sign}.
Parseval and \cref{eq:correlation} give $\sum_{a,b}\widetilde C[a,b]=1$
and the expansion of $\widetilde H_i$ in Claim~\ref{heavy:claim-endpoint}.
For nonnegative integers $p,l$ with $p+l\ge1$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and
$0\le\rho<1$, we use
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:gram-bound}
 \sum_{a\ge p}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}|q_a^{(l)}(s)|^2
 \le\frac{2(2p+2l-3)!!}{\pi(1-\rho^2)^{p+l-1/2}}.
\end{equation}
For $j=0$, Parseval and \cref{heavy:gram-bound} with $l=0$ give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a\ge p,b\ge0}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}\widetilde C[a,b]
 &=\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{a\ge p}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}
 \left|q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(X_i)\right)\right|^2\right]\\
 &\le\frac{2(2p-3)!!}{\pi(1-\rho^2)^{p-1/2}}
 \qquad(1\le p\le4).
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $a\ge0$, $|\alpha|=j\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, and
$\beta\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^3$, Taylor expansion and Gaussian integration
by parts using $(\phi\operatorname{He}_n)'=-\phi\operatorname{He}_{n+1}$ give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \partial^\alpha q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(x_i)\right)
 &=\sum_{l=1}^{|\alpha|}B_{\alpha,l}(x)
 q_a^{(l)}\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(x_i)\right),\\
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\partial^\alpha q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(X_i)\right)
 \psi_\beta(X)\right]
 &=\sqrt{\frac{(\beta+\alpha)!}{\beta!}}\,
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(X_i)\right)
 \psi_{\beta+\alpha}(X)\right],\\
 \sum_{|\alpha|=j}\frac{j!}{\alpha!}
 \left\|\partial^\alpha q_a\!\left(\sum_i\widetilde r(X_i)\right)\right\|_2^2
 &=\sum_b(b)_j\widetilde C[a,b],
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last equality follows from Parseval and
$\sum_{|\alpha|=j}(j!/\alpha!)\prod_i(\beta_i)_{\alpha_i}=(|\beta|)_j$.
Boundedness of $\widetilde r,\ldots,\widetilde r^{(4)}$ and
\cref{head:smoothed-sign} justify integration by parts. The triangle inequality gives
\[
 \left(\sum_{a\ge p,b\ge j}(a)_p(b)_j\rho^{a-p}\widetilde C[a,b]\right)^{1/2}
 \le\sum_{l=1}^j\left(T_{j,l}\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}
 \sum_{a\ge p}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}|q_a^{(l)}(s)|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Apply \cref{heavy:gram-bound}; finite sums and monotone convergence
justify summation over $a$.

For \cref{heavy:gram-bound}, with $u,v\in\mathbb R$ and $n=p+l-1$, use
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:gram-identity}
 \sum_{a\ge p}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}q_a^{(l)}(u)q_a^{(l)}(v)
 =4\partial_u^n\partial_v^n
 \frac{e^{-(u^2-2\rho uv+v^2)/(2(1-\rho^2))}}
 {2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}.
\end{equation}
Fourier inversion, Cauchy--Schwarz, and the Gaussian moment formula give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 4\left|\partial_u^n\partial_v^n
 \frac{e^{-(u^2-2\rho uv+v^2)/(2(1-\rho^2))}}
 {2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right|
 &\le\frac1{\pi^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}|\xi\eta|^n
 e^{-(\xi^2+2\rho\xi\eta+\eta^2)/2}\,d\xi\,d\eta\\
 &\le\frac1{\pi^2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\xi^{2n}
 e^{-(\xi^2+2\rho\xi\eta+\eta^2)/2}\,d\xi\,d\eta
 =\frac{2(2n-1)!!}{\pi(1-\rho^2)^{n+1/2}}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Setting $u=v=s$ proves \cref{heavy:gram-bound}. To prove
\cref{heavy:gram-identity}, use \cref{head:smoothed-sign},
$(\phi\operatorname{He}_j)'=-\phi\operatorname{He}_{j+1}$, and Mehler's identity:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a\ge p}(a)_p\rho^{a-p}q_a^{(l)}(u)q_a^{(l)}(v)
 &=4\phi(u)\phi(v)\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\rho^k}{k!}
 \operatorname{He}_{k+n}(u)\operatorname{He}_{k+n}(v)\\
 &=4\partial_u^n\partial_v^n
 \left(\phi(u)\phi(v)\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\rho^k}{k!}\operatorname{He}_k(u)\operatorname{He}_k(v)\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
At $\rho=0$, only $a=p$ remains. For $0<\rho<1$ and arbitrary
nonnegative integer shifts $p,l$, termwise differentiation is justified
locally uniformly in $u,v\in\mathbb R$ by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\rho^k}{k!}|\operatorname{He}_{k+p}(u)\operatorname{He}_{k+l}(v)|\\
 &\quad\le\left(\sup_{k\ge0}\frac{\sqrt{(k+p)!(k+l)!}}{k!}\rho^{k/2}\right)
 \left(\sum_{k\ge0}\rho^{k/2}\psi_{k+p}(u)^2\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{k\ge0}\rho^{k/2}\psi_{k+l}(v)^2\right)^{1/2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For fixed $p,l$ and $0<\rho<1$,
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{(k+p)!(k+l)!}}{k!}\rho^{k/2}
 \le(k+p+l+1)^{(p+l)/2}\rho^{k/2}\longrightarrow0\quad(k\to\infty).
\]
Mehler's identity with equal arguments gives
\[
 \sum_{k\ge0}\rho^{k/2}\psi_{k+p}(u)^2
 \le\frac{\rho^{-p/2}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}
 \exp\!\left(\frac{\sqrt\rho\,u^2}{1+\sqrt\rho}\right).
\]
Apply the preceding sum inequality to tails. The displayed limit and
these bounds for $(p,u)$ and $(l,v)$ give uniform convergence on compact
sets of $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$.

Each monomial of $B_{\alpha,l}^2$ contains $2l\le8$ derivative factors.
Independence factors its expectation into one-dimensional moments. For each such moment,
with $k\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^4$ and $1\le|k|\le8$, parity and vanishing derivatives give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\int_\mathbb{R}\prod_{h=1}^4(\widetilde r^{(h)}(x))^{k_h}\phi(x)\,dx\\
 &=\left(1+(-1)^{\sum_h(h+1)k_h}\right)
 \left(\int_0^{27/4}\prod_{h=1}^4(r^{(h)}(x))^{k_h}\phi(x)\,dx +\int_0^{1/4}\prod_{h=1}^4(\widetilde r^{(h)}(27/4+u))^{k_h}
 \phi(27/4+u)\,du\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The moment with $|k|=0$ is $1$. On each integration interval,
$\deg\widetilde r^{(h)}\le25$ for $1\le h\le4$, so each product has degree
at most $25|k|\le200$. For $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $l\ge0$, and integer $k\ge1$,
Gaussian integration gives
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:gaussian-moments}
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_0^l\phi(a+u)\,du
 &=\tfrac12[\operatorname{erfc}(a/\sqrt2)-\operatorname{erfc}((a+l)/\sqrt2)],\\
 \int_0^l u\phi(a+u)\,du
 &=\phi(a)-\phi(a+l)-a\int_0^l\phi(a+u)\,du,\\
 \int_0^l u^{k+1}\phi(a+u)\,du
 &=k\int_0^l u^{k-1}\phi(a+u)\,du
 -a\int_0^l u^k\phi(a+u)\,du-l^k\phi(a+l)\quad(k\ge1).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $(a,l)=(0,27/4),(27/4,1/4)$, these recurrences and
\cref{heavy:cap-definition}, evaluated with interval rounding at $1536$
bits, give the strict bounds in \cref{heavy:T-definition}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\Re((1\pm z)^{-1})>0$, we use
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:mass-single}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\left|
 \frac{e^{-u^2/(2(1+z))-v^2/(2(1-z))}}
 {2\pi\sqrt{(1+z)(1-z)}}\right|\,du\,dv
 =\left(|1-z^2|\Re((1+z)^{-1})\Re((1-z)^{-1})\right)^{-1/2},
\end{equation}
and the coefficient identity
\[
 4![\epsilon^4]\exp\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^4\frac{\ell_k(Y)}{k!}\epsilon^k\right)
 =\ell_1^4+6\ell_1^2\ell_2+3\ell_2^2+4\ell_1\ell_3+\ell_4.
\]
The right-hand side equals the fourth derivative in $\epsilon$ at
$\epsilon=0$ of the product density at correlations
$P_i(te^\epsilon),-te^\epsilon,-te^\epsilon,-te^\epsilon$, divided by
that product density at $\epsilon=0$. The integration coordinates
$W,W',X,X'$ are held fixed. Since $|\widetilde F|\le1$, Cauchy--Schwarz and
\[
 \Re((1\pm e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta})^{-1})=\tfrac12,\qquad
 |1-e^{2{\mathrm{i}}\theta}|=2\sin\theta\quad(0<\theta<\pi)
\]
give \cref{heavy:score-bound}. On a sufficiently small bounded complex
neighborhood of the compact arc, the closure satisfies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Re((1\pm P_i(t))^{-1})
 &\ge\frac12\inf_{\theta\in I}\Re((1\pm P_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}))^{-1})>0,\\
 \Re((1\pm t)^{-1})&\ge\frac14.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Each of the first four $\mathcal D$-derivatives of the product density
is that density times a polynomial of degree at most eight in
$W,W',X,X'$, with coefficients bounded on this neighborhood. The density
and these derivatives are therefore bounded by a constant multiple of
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left(1+W^2+(W')^2+\sum_{j=1}^3(X_j^2+(X'_j)^2)\right)^4\\
 &\quad\cdot\exp\!\Biggl[-\frac14
 \min\left\{\frac12,\inf_{\substack{\theta\in I\\\sigma=\pm1}}
 \Re((1+\sigma P_i(e^{{\mathrm{i}}\theta}))^{-1})\right\}\cdot
 \left(W^2+(W')^2+\sum_{j=1}^3(X_j^2+(X'_j)^2)\right)\Biggr].
 \end{aligned}
\]
This integrable bound is independent of $t$ in that neighborhood.
Differentiation under the integral therefore gives the analytic
continuation of $\widetilde H_i$.

To verify \cref{heavy:mass-single}, integrate the absolute density
separately in $u,v$. After normalization,
\[
 \sqrt{\Re((1+z)^{-1})}u,\qquad\sqrt{\Re((1-z)^{-1})}v
\]
are independent standard Gaussians. Thus $Y_{0,\pm}$ are their individual squares and
$Y_{1,\pm}$ sums of three such squares, proving the stated independence
and moment-generating functions. The Gaussian change of variables is
made at $\epsilon=0$, after differentiation at fixed $W,W',X,X'$;
hence $Y$ and $\Re((1+\sigma P_i(t))^{-1})$ remain fixed as required in
\cref{heavy:ell}. The logarithm of the product density at correlations
$P_i(te^\epsilon),-te^\epsilon,-te^\epsilon,-te^\epsilon$
gives \cref{heavy:ell}. The expansions
\[
 \ln(1+u)=\sum_{h=1}^4\frac{(-1)^{h+1}}h u^h+O(u^5),\qquad
 (1+u)^{-1}=\sum_{h=0}^4(-u)^h+O(u^5)
\]
apply to the two arguments in \cref{heavy:ell} after factoring
$1+\sigma P_i(t)$ and $1-\sigma t$, respectively, with
\[
 u=\frac{\sigma(P_i(te^\epsilon)-P_i(t))}{1+\sigma P_i(t)}
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 u=\frac{-\sigma t(e^\epsilon-1)}{1-\sigma t}.
\]
To evaluate the expectation in \cref{heavy:score-bound}, in the rest
of this proof set
\[
 \alpha=(1/2,1/2,3/2,3/2),\qquad
 (Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,Y_4)=(Y_{0,+},Y_{0,-},Y_{1,+},Y_{1,-}).
\]
Define
\[
 Q_{\alpha_h,k}(y):=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj(-2)^{k-j}
 \left(\prod_{l=j}^{k-1}(\alpha_h+l)\right)y^j
 \qquad(1\le h\le4,\ k\ge0),
\]
with empty products one; $[y^k]Q_{\alpha_h,k}(y)=1$.
For nonnegative integers $j,k,n$, we use
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:laguerre}
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[Q_{\alpha_h,k}(Y_h)Q_{\alpha_h,j}(Y_h)]
 &=\mathbf1_{k=j}4^kk!\prod_{l=0}^{k-1}(\alpha_h+l),\\
 Y_h^n&=\sum_{k=0}^n2^{n-k}\binom nk
 \left(\prod_{l=k}^{n-1}(\alpha_h+l)\right)Q_{\alpha_h,k}(Y_h).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $k\in\{0,1,\ldots\}^4$, $|k|\le4$, set
\[
 p_k:=\frac{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[
 (\ell_1^4+6\ell_1^2\ell_2+3\ell_2^2+4\ell_1\ell_3+\ell_4)
 \prod_{h=1}^4Q_{\alpha_h,k_h}(Y_h)\right]}
 {\prod_{h=1}^4\left(4^{k_h}k_h!\prod_{j=0}^{k_h-1}(\alpha_h+j)\right)}.
\]
Since $\deg_Y\ell_j\le1$ for $1\le j\le4$, independence and
\cref{heavy:laguerre} give
\begin{equation}\label{heavy:score-norm}
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|\ell_1^4+6\ell_1^2\ell_2+3\ell_2^2+4\ell_1\ell_3+\ell_4|^2
 =\sum_{|k|\le4}|p_k|^2
 \prod_{h=1}^4\left(4^{k_h}k_h!\prod_{j=0}^{k_h-1}(\alpha_h+j)\right).
\end{equation}
For \cref{heavy:laguerre}, use
\[
 \sum_{k\ge0}Q_{\alpha_h,k}(y)\frac{z^k}{k!}
 =(1+2z)^{-\alpha_h}\exp\!\left(\frac{yz}{1+2z}\right)
 \qquad(|z|<1/2).
\]
The moment-generating functions in Claim~\ref{heavy:claim-arc} give
\[
 \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[
 \frac{\exp\!\left(Y_h\left(\frac{u}{1+2u}+\frac{v}{1+2v}\right)\right)}
 {(1+2u)^{\alpha_h}(1+2v)^{\alpha_h}}\right]
 =(1-4uv)^{-\alpha_h}.
\]
For $|u|,|v|<1/8$, the integrand is bounded by
$(4/3)^{2\alpha_h}e^{Y_h/3}$, with finite expectation
$(4/3)^{2\alpha_h}3^{\alpha_h}$. Taking $k!j![u^kv^j]$ under the
expectation proves orthogonality. Substitution $z=s/(1-2s)$ gives
\[
 e^{sY_h}=\sum_{k\ge0}
 \frac{Q_{\alpha_h,k}(Y_h)s^k}{k!(1-2s)^{\alpha_h+k}};
\]
taking $n![s^n]$ proves the second identity.
